model.description: Every business, amount and payment date in these scenarios is invented. They illustrate cash timing, not typical Australian business performance.
model.convention: Day 0 is starting cash. Days 1–30 show the end-of-day balance after netting all receipts and payments on that day. This can hide an intraday shortfall.
model.depositConvention: A hypothetical agreed deposit arrives on day 1. It reduces the selected customer’s later payment by exactly the same amount. It is not extra revenue, and acceptance is not guaranteed.
model.bufferConvention: Opening buffer is additional hypothetical cash already available at the start. The model does not assume borrowing or explain how that cash is obtained.
model.negativeBalanceMeaning: A negative balance is an unfunded gap in this scenario. It does not mean an overdraft or other credit is available.
model.horizonConvention: A delayed receipt after day 30 is reported separately. It is not included in the closing balance and is not assumed lost.
model.limits: Amounts represent final cash movements. No GST or other tax calculation, interest, borrowing cost, legal payment deadline, eligibility assessment or personalised recommendation is modelled. Unlisted receipts, costs and obligations are omitted. Closing cash is not profit.
model.sourceScope: The official sources support the cash-flow principles only. They do not supply or validate the invented scenario amounts, dates or deposit percentages.

scenarios.title: The late customer
scenarios.description: The month can finish with A$8,000 even though an earlier payment cannot be covered. Move one customer payment and inspect the lowest balance.
scenarios.prompt: Can a positive closing balance hide an earlier cash gap?
scenarios.lesson: With no extra buffer or deposit, cash first falls below zero on day 7. A 15-day delay deepens the minimum from −A$1,000 to −A$7,000 while day-30 cash remains A$8,000.

scenarios.title: The growing order
scenarios.description: A new order adds A$20,000 of receipts and A$16,000 of specified payments, but the payments come first. Try a hypothetical deposit agreed before work begins.
scenarios.prompt: Why can an order that adds cash by month-end deepen the earlier gap?
scenarios.lesson: The order adds A$4,000 to closing cash after its two specified payments, but creates a minimum balance of −A$9,000. A 45% deposit moves A$9,000 to day 1 and removes that gap. This is a timing example, not a recommended deposit rate or a full profit calculation.

scenarios.title: The lumpy costs
scenarios.description: A$20,000 arrives and A$18,000 leaves during the month, but rent and an equipment payment arrive before most receipts. Monthly totals hide the concentration.
scenarios.prompt: Does A$2,000 more coming in than going out mean every payment is covered?
scenarios.lesson: The monthly net inflow is positive, yet the lowest daily balance is −A$6,000. Even moving 50% of the project invoice to day 1 leaves an A$1,000 gap. Starting cash, payment timing and monthly totals answer different questions.
